What makes Roman special: • Its mirror came from hardware once built for U.S. intelligence • Same mirror size as Hubble, but less than 1/4 the weight • A huge 300MP infrared camera • Each image covers at least 100× more sky than Hubble • In five years, it should image over 50× more sky than Hubble did in 30 • Will study dark matter, dark energy and billions of galaxies • Carries 1,350,144 people’s names toward L2 • All survey data will be public after processing Roman launched nine months early and on budget. moments.selftext: “Everybody wants to save the Earth; nobody wants to help Mom do the dishes.” - P.J. O'Rourke This famous quote points to a common flaw in human nature: our tendency to become inspired by grand, heroic causes while overlooking the small, practical responsibilities directly in front of us. People can easily rally around enormous, abstract goals like saving the planet because they feel noble, exciting, and meaningful. Yet true character and kindness are often revealed through the ordinary, repetitive moments of everyday life. Washing the dishes or helping a family member may seem insignificant, but these quiet acts require effort without recognition, applause, or public attention. Ultimately, the quote offers a humorous but pointed reminder that making the world a better place often begins with simple acts of responsibility and genuine kindness within our own homes.

moments.title: Steve Irwin’s final moments were recorded on camera. His close friend and longtime producer, John Stainton, fought to keep the footage private, and to this day, it has never been released to the public. Steve Irwin died
moments.selftext: Steve Irwin’s final moments were recorded on camera. His close friend and longtime producer, John Stainton, fought to keep the footage private, and to this day, it has never been released to the public. Steve Irwin died on Sept. 4, 2006, while filming the documentary Ocean’s Deadliest near Australia’s Great Barrier Reef. During a break in production, Irwin and cameraman Justin Lyons entered shallow water to film a large stingray for a separate television project featuring Irwin’s daughter, Bindi. As Irwin approached the animal, the stingray suddenly lifted its tail and struck him repeatedly in the chest. Lyons continued filming because the crew had been instructed to keep the cameras running whenever someone was in danger. Once Irwin was brought back onto the boat, the camera was turned off. Despite efforts to save him, his injuries were fatal. The footage was handed over to authorities as part of the official investigation. John Stainton, Irwin’s close friend and longtime producer, strongly opposed its public release, describing the recording as deeply disturbing. Accounts of what happened to the footage afterward have varied, although Terri Irwin later stated that it was destroyed once the investigation was complete. The footage has never been released to the public, preserving Irwin’s dignity and allowing him to be remembered for his extraordinary life and passion for wildlife rather than the circumstances of his death. According to Lyons, Irwin’s final words were, “I’m dying.”

Anthropic did disclose the weekly limits on its own website in 2025: Max 5x ($100): 140–280 hours of Sonnet Max 20x ($200): 240–480 hours of Sonnet So the $200 plan cost twice as much, but offered only around 1.7x the expected weekly Sonnet usage. moments.title: We need to talk about Anthropic. Its relationship with its power users appears to be collapsing in real time. A few weeks ago, my post about Claude becoming lazy and failing at basic agentic tasks received 2.5 million vi
moments.selftext: We need to talk about Anthropic. Its relationship with its power users appears to be collapsing in real time. A few weeks ago, my post about Claude becoming lazy and failing at basic agentic tasks received 2.5 million views and more than 2,000 replies, with the overwhelming majority of commenters agreeing. This weekend, Anthropic framed a 17% reduction in current weekly usage as a “permanent 25% increase.” It deleted the original announcement, reposted it with an explanation, and still received a Community Note. Today, users discovered that the $200 “Max 20x” plan only provides 20x usage within a five-hour window. Its weekly allowance appears to be only roughly twice that of the $100 plan. Anthropic is already facing a proposed class-action lawsuit over these limits. Meanwhile, Claude is going viral for ending a session after a user repeatedly insulted it. Claude may be the only $ 200-a-month product where the agent regularly fails to finish the job, nobody can tell you exactly how much usage you have bought, and the product can decide that it no longer wants to work with you. Employees like @trq212 take these concerns seriously and genuinely ask for honest feedback, which I really appreciate. I have always found Anthropic’s staff to be friendly and respectful. But Anthropic’s public communication is very poor right now, and its models are also performing poorly in terms of practical usability. Fable is the exception, but its rate limits make it almost impossible to use consistently. I am genuinely trying to understand the underlying issue, but I honestly cannot come up with a convincing explanation. Anthropic set out to be the highly ethical AI company, a position that ultimately led to its clash with the DoD. But the idea that this philosophy should extend to Claude ending sessions because it objects to a user’s tone is baffling to me. Frankly, it is a deal-breaker. An AI needs to be able to handle my frustration. After all, it is not a person who can actually be offended. Anthropic is reportedly preparing for an IPO. Given that, it is even more puzzling that the company does not appear to be making an all-out effort to improve its public image. Anthropic is making things remarkably easy for the competition right now.
